messages:
Alex K: IA-Detector flagged a weird chain — same SSO session token observed hopping through three distinct public IPs across different countries in ~4m. MFA prompts spiked for the same user pool. Seeing some account lockouts after repeated pushes. Noticed at 14:12 UTC.
Maria S: Can you dump the affected user IDs and IP list? Curious if this is automated proxy rotation or a compromised session being passed around.
Samir L: Running a quick query now. Query: ```select user_id, ip, geo, ts from sso_events where session_token='tok:***abc' and ts between 1700000000 and 1700002400 order by ts;``` will post results in a sec.
IA-Detector Bot: ALERT 1887654321: session_handoff_chain detected. confidence=0.86. hops=3. ips=[185.92.45.12, 41.76.8.9, 203.0.113.77]. first_seen=14:08Z last_seen=14:12Z. matched_signals=[mfa_prompt_spike, unusual_geolocation_sequence]
Samir L: Quick result sample: ```user: jade.c@redwood.com | ips: 185.92.45.12 -> 41.76.8.9 -> 203.0.113.77 | events: mfa:prompt x6, login:success, session_resume``` (redacting full list for thread). Looks like multiple employees and one service account.
DevOps Oncall: Any indication of token theft vs forwarded header abuse from our SSO proxy? If headers are proxied, we need to check the X-Forwarded-For chain and our trust list.
Alex K: Good point. Samir, can you check `x-forwarded-for` vs `client_ip` in logs for those requests? Also verify SAML assertion issuer IDs and agent fingerprints.
Samir L: Checking. Preliminary: SAML issuer OK, assertion signature valid. But I see alternating `user_agent` strings like `Mozilla/5.0` then `curl/7.68` then `python-requests/2.25`. Looks scripted. XFF shows internal LB -> tor exit -> unknown -> public proxy. So likely chained proxy.
Maria S: If it's scripted automated handoff, MFA fatigue might be the goal — repeated prompts until user approves. Any evidence of push acceptance pattern? e.g., repeated push prompts then eventual success.
Samir L: Yes — timeline: push x5 over 3 minutes, then a `passwordless` session_resume. For one account, `mfa:approved` appears right after the chain. Could be social engineered approve or exposed backup codes.
Chris P: Recommend containment: 1) force session invalidate for affected tokens, 2) revoke refresh tokens for impacted users, 3) force re-auth + block suspect IPs. Thoughts?
DevOps Oncall: Agreed. We can push session flush via `/admin/sessions/invalidate` for token list. Also add IPs to temporary blocklist in WAF for 1h while we triage.
Jade C: I'm on the list — I did get repeated push prompts but I dismissed them. Didn't approve any. Thanks for the heads up.
Alex K: Action plan: Samir, export full affected token list and user emails. DevOps Oncall, schedule immediate session invalidate for those tokens and add WAF blocks for the three IPs. Maria, coordinate comms to CS for any impacted customer accounts and prepare internal advisory. Chris, we need a follow-up post-incident note with root cause and mitigations.
Samir L: Exported and uploaded to secure share: /secure/incidents/1887654321/affected_tokens.csv (link: https://vault.internal/secure/incidents/1887654321). Including fields: user_email, token_id, ip_chain, first_seen, last_seen, mfa_events_count.
IA-Detector Bot: Note: additional ~12 similar sessions detected with lower confidence in last 30m. Recommend sweep for same fingerprints.
DevOps Oncall: Kicked off session invalidate job at 14:22Z, WAF block pushed at 14:24Z. Monitoring for reattempts.
Maria S: CS notified at 14:27Z — Jade and two other employees flagged. Draft for internal: "If you received unexpected MFA prompts do NOT approve; contact security@redwood immediately." Sending now.
Chris P: Post-incident actions: add stricter rate limits on MFA prompts per account, enforce push prompt context (location/device) UI, log XFF chains into audit log, and run a retro for SSO proxy trust boundaries. I'll create a GH ticket after this thread.
Alex K: Thanks team. Keep updates minimal here — move detailed logs to the incident folder. We'll schedule 1hr review at 15:00Z. :lock:
